title: Bags lost their crunch: diagnosing storage failures
description: Freeze-dried food that went soft, stale, or off in storage failed at one of five points: dryness, packaging, absorber, seal, or environment. Find yours.
author: Jack Ferrence

sources.title: How to Store Freeze-Dried Food in Mylar Bags

faq.question: Why did my stored freeze-dried food go soft, stale, or off?
faq.answer: Freeze-dried food that went soft, stale, or off in storage failed at one of five points: dryness, packaging, absorber, seal, or environment. Find yours.

howTo.name: 1. The food was never dry enough
howTo.text: Before any recovery step: a texture problem is a quality signal and cannot establish that food is safe to eat. Confirm how the food was handled — fully dry and sealed in a working barrier going in, kept cool, dark and dry since, seal still intact, never warmed or left open, and containing nothing that was perishable before drying. Freeze-drying does not kill pathogens. Where any of those answers is unknown, discard the food rather than recover it. Start here because it is the cheapest thing to rule out, not because it is the most frequent — nobody publishes failure rankings for home batches, including us. Food that passed a casual glance but not a real cut test carries moisture into the bag, where it equalizes and softens everything. Check: open a suspect bag and cut-test several pieces. Uniform slight softness across the bag points to residual moisture, not a leak. Fix: tighten your end-of-cycle dryness testing so the next batch does not repeat it. Whether this food can be dried again and re-bagged is decided by the handling answers above, not by the texture in front of you.

howTo.name: 2. The packaging wasn’t a real barrier
howTo.text: Zip-top bags, thin food-saver plastic, and decorative pouches are not long-term freeze-dry storage — they pass moisture and oxygen slowly but relentlessly. The standard is mylar in the 5–7.5 mil range with a metallized barrier layer, mason jars vacuum-sealed, or PETE with absorbers. Thin printed pouches sold for candy resale are fine for weeks of retail turnover, not years of pantry. Fix: match packaging to intended life: barrier mylar for storage, and inform retail customers of a realistic best-by window.

howTo.name: 3. The oxygen absorber was spent or undersized
howTo.text: Absorbers die in open air: a bowl of absorbers left out during a long bagging session is a bowl of warm iron filings. Sizing matters too: roughly 100 cc per quart of container volume (300–500 cc for a one-gallon bag), erring high because freeze-dried food is airy. Check: not by the look of the bag. PackFreshUSA, who supply these bags, call the “vacuum-packed look” a common misconception — you will often see a bag draw in, but not seeing it does not mean the oxygen removal failed. Cut-test the contents of a suspect bag instead. Fix: buy absorbers in small sealed packs, open one pack per session, and reseal spares immediately.

howTo.name: 4. The seal itself leaked
howTo.text: A wrinkle, a crumb, or a stray thread of candy in the seal line is a slow leak with a years-long fuse. Check: press gently on the bag and watch the seal line; inspect for channels. Fix: seal wide and wrinkle-free, wipe the seal area before closing, double-seal high-value bags, and spot-check each session’s output the next day.

howTo.name: 5. The environment beat the packaging
howTo.text: Even good packaging loses eventually to heat and light. Guidance converges on storage below 70 °F, dark, and dry : a closet, not a garage that hits 95 °F all summer. High-fat foods deserve special mention: fat oxidizes regardless of moisture control, so bacon-adjacent experiments and oily leftovers have inherently short horizons; extension guidance flags high-fat foods as poor freeze-drying candidates in the first place.

howTo.name: The one-day-later habit
howTo.text: Twenty-four hours after packaging, walk the day’s bags: each should be slightly drawn in, seals clean, contents audibly crisp when tilted. That single check catches spent absorbers, seal channels, and wet batches while they’re still one batch — log it as a pass/fail in your Batch Log and storage failures become rare events instead of sad discoveries.

bodyHtml:
A batch that was perfect on packaging day and soft three months later failed at one of exactly five points. Work down the list, and if you sell, treat every failed bag as a process defect to trace, because your customers’ bags came off the same table.

Before any of this: what do you know about how the food was handled? A texture problem is a quality signal. It cannot tell you whether food is safe to eat, and neither can drying it again. Answer these first, and if you cannot answer them, discard the food rather than recover it: was it fully dry and sealed with a working barrier when it went into storage; has it stayed cool, dark and dry since; is the seal still intact; did it ever warm, sweat or sit open; and does it contain meat, fish, dairy, egg or anything else that was perishable before it was dried? Freeze-drying does not kill pathogens, so nothing that was unsafe going in becomes safe by coming out. When any answer is “I don’t know,” the food is not a candidate for recovery. If a product was sold, or is destined to be, your state’s Department of Agriculture or health department decides what may be reworked — not this page.

1. The food was never dry enough

Start here because it is the cheapest thing to rule out, not because it is the most frequent — nobody publishes failure rankings for home batches, including us. Food that passed a casual glance but not a real cut test carries moisture into the bag, where it equalizes and softens everything. Check: open a suspect bag and cut-test several pieces. Uniform slight softness across the bag points to residual moisture, not a leak. Fix: the process fix is to tighten your end-of-cycle dryness testing so the next batch does not repeat it. Whether this food can be dried again and re-bagged is a separate question, and the handling answers above decide it — not the texture in front of you.

2. The packaging wasn’t a real barrier

Zip-top bags, thin food-saver plastic, and decorative pouches are not long-term freeze-dry storage — they pass moisture and oxygen slowly but relentlessly. The standard is mylar in the 5–7.5 mil range with a metallized barrier layer, mason jars vacuum-sealed, or PETE with absorbers. Thin printed pouches sold for candy resale are fine for weeks of retail turnover, not years of pantry. Fix: match packaging to intended life: barrier mylar for storage, and inform retail customers of a realistic best-by window.

3. The oxygen absorber was spent or undersized

Absorbers begin reacting the moment the packet is opened, so a bowl of them left out across a long bagging session is losing capacity the whole time. How much, and how fast, our supplier does not publish, and neither will we — the point is that the exposure is avoidable, not that a given packet is provably dead. Sizing matters too: roughly 100 cc per quart of container volume (300–500 cc for a one-gallon bag), erring high because freeze-dried food is airy. Check: not by the look of the bag. PackFreshUSA, whose absorbers and bags this site sells, calls the “vacuum-packed look” a common misconception: you will often see a bag draw in, but not seeing it does not mean the oxygen removal failed. Judge the food instead — cut-test contents from a suspect bag — and treat packet handling as the controllable variable. Fix: buy absorbers in small sealed packs, open one pack per session, and reseal spares immediately.

4. The seal itself leaked

A wrinkle, a crumb, or a stray thread of candy in the seal line is a slow leak with a years-long fuse. Check: press gently on the bag and watch the seal line; inspect for channels. Fix: seal wide and wrinkle-free, wipe the seal area before closing, double-seal high-value bags, and spot-check each session’s output the next day.

5. The environment beat the packaging

Even good packaging loses eventually to heat and light. Guidance converges on storage below 70 °F, dark, and dry: a closet, not a garage that hits 95 °F all summer. High-fat foods deserve special mention: fat oxidizes regardless of moisture control, so bacon-adjacent experiments and oily leftovers have inherently short horizons; extension guidance flags high-fat foods as poor freeze-drying candidates in the first place.

The one-day-later habit

Twenty-four hours after packaging, walk the day’s bags: seals clean and unwrinkled, contents audibly crisp when tilted. Some bags will have drawn in and some will not, and per PackFreshUSA that difference on its own proves nothing either way — so read the seal line and the contents, not the shape. Log it as a pass/fail in your Batch Log: a habit that surfaces a problem while it is still one batch is worth keeping even when it does not catch everything.
